content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors suggested using the kNN method to improve the prediction of drug-target binding affinity. Both kNN-DTA and the extended Ada-kNN-DTA achieved better retrieval performance in several benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. Strengths: The importance of the problem studied in the paper is justifiable. The authors used a very simple method to get SOTA performance for the critical DTA problem, which reflects the positive aspect of the paper.  Also, the results seem to be quite superior compared to the baselines.

2. Weakness: However, the writing quality of the paper really undermines the credibility of the paper's contributions. 
    1. Mathematical formulations: In the 'Preliminary' section, the definition of DTA dataset is not appropriately introduced. The author(s) mentioned 'y (a floating number)'. At least, the domain of the elements of this DTA dataset should be carefully defined. A similar issue lies on 'Datastore'. I am not sure if this is really a rigorous term corresponding to some mathematical object or something else.

Same issue for 'another 1 point gain'.  Also, examples such as '... proposed two aggregation and retrieval ways,  ... Though hot and popular ...,  ...by more than one point w.r.t. RMSE and R.' do not reflect the quality of a standard scientific paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer GJwX
content.comment:
Thanks for your review comments and we are sorry to make you feel so unhappy about the writing. Here we give some discussions. 

> **Mathematical formulations: In the 'Preliminary' section, the definition of DTA dataset is not appropriately introduced. The author(s) mentioned 'y (a floating number)'. At least, the domain of the elements of this DTA dataset should be carefully defined. A similar issue lies on 'Datastore'. I am not sure if this is really a rigorous term corresponding to some mathematical object or something else.**

**A**:  Thanks for raising the question. 
* The definition of y is a floating number, which stands for the binding affinity score (e.g., Ki, IC50). The detailed domain of y is determined by the specific dataset, and we have shown the distribution of y in Appendix A.1 (figure 3). For example, the affinity values in Davis range from $5.0$ to $10.8$, and the KIBA affinity scores range from $0.0$ to $17.2$, BinddingDB IC50 and KI range from $2.0$ to $11.0$. Therefore, we feel it is not appropriate to describe these details in the main text due to space limitations. We have added and updated Appendix A.1.
* As for “Datastore”, we are following previous works (e.g., $k$NN-LM [1] and $k$NN-MT [2]) in NLP to describe the pre-saved drug/target representations. Kindly check the previous works, we have made a consistent description instead of randomly creating terms by ourselves. 

> **Unclear or less rigorous explanations: 'obtains new records of RMSE scores 0.687 and 0.748 with both 4 point improvement.' What does it mean by '4 point improvement'? Same issue for 'another 1 point gain'. Also, examples such as '... proposed two aggregation and retrieval ways, ... Though hot and popular ..., ...by more than one point w.r.t. RMSE and R.' do not reflect the quality of a standard scientific paper.**

**A**:  Sorry to make you feel unclear about these parts. For the “4 points improvement”, this is the description when we compare the results of our kNN-DTA and the pre-trained DTA model (see Table 1). Specifically, we mean $0.687$ RMSE is better than $0.726$ RMSE, and the reduced RMSE score is about $4$ points (in percentile). This may be acceptable for “ML” papers (may not be scientific papers). But as you pointed out, we have revised these descriptions and other sentences that you mentioned to be clearer. We are grateful that the reviewer can provide other cases if you feel unsatisfied and we will revise them. 

> **Novelty and reproducibility: The novelty is okay and It is difficult to evaluate its reproducibility because there aren't codes in the supplement and implementation details are not fully presented in the paper.**

**A**: Thanks for the suggestion. We provide the code on github: https://github.com/kNN-DTA/kNN-DTA. In our initial submission, we feel our method is simple yet effective so just ignore open-source implementation. We have provided it now for reproduction. 
___
We will continue revising our paper writing, though we have used some tools such as Grammarly to help check the paper there remains room for improvement. Nevertheless, we think our paper can be understood in general and we will continue improving. We kindly hope that the reviewer can also consider the method and the effectiveness/verification in balance to reassess our work. We hope our continued revising can help remove your concerns. 
___

[1] Urvashi Khandelwal, Omer Levy, Dan Jurafsky, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Mike Lewis. Generalization through memorization: Nearest neighbor language models. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2019.

[2] Urvashi Khandelwal, Angela Fan, Dan Jurafsky, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Mike Lewis. Nearest neighbor machine translation. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a drug-target-affinity model which is mainly based on two pre-trained transformer encoders, which create embeddings for the input compound and protein, and the k-nearest neighbors algorithm to perform retrieval steps from an external memory. The model includes two different retrieval mechanisms. Firstly, similarities between the input and the knn memory instances, i.e. a compound-protein-combination, are used as weights, such that a affinity prediction can be computed as a weighted sum over the labels of the nearest neighbors. Secondly, the embeddings of the input compound and protein is enriched by associating them with an external compound and protein memory. The authors evaluate their model on BindingDB, KIBA and DAVIS.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- [+, S1] Predicting affinity from molecular and protein input is an important problem setting in drug discovery. Applying external memories and retrieval based methods in this field is a promising research direction.
- [+, S2] knn-DTA and Ada-knn-DTA outperform the other baseline methods presented in the paper.
- [+, S3] The appendix gives insights to different hyperparameter effects.
- [-, W1] Error bars and statistical tests are not included.
- [-, W2] Some of the recently best performing PCM models are not included in the results section.
- [-, W3] The authors neglect huge parts of the litearture which are related to machine learning models using external memories.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Quality - [-, W1] Error bars and statistical tests are not included. Therefore, performance-wise differences could just arrise by chance which is why the presented results are not relevant. The authors should follow best practices and include error bars and statistical tests. - [-, W2] Similarity based PCM methods have shown to yield strong performances. Unfortunately, some methods are missing in the evaluation which is why it is unclear whether the proposed architecture reaches state-of-the-art. The authors should include relevant methods such as [1-4] - [-, W3] The authors missed to refer to recent Machine Learning literature which deals with external memory based methods such as [5-7]. The authors should add relevant literature and explain why they decided to use KNNs. More sophisticated ML methods for external memories might even boost the overall performance. This seems underexplored. ### Clarity - The parts about the retrieval steps, which build the core of the architecture, are well-written and understandable. - The clarity is diminished since the authors missed to explain the prediction module in the main paper. The authors should include information here (or point the reviewer to referring passages in case the reviewer missed relevant parts). - Pre-Training / Fine-tuning unclarity: In 4.1, the precise training procedure remains unclear. The authors should describe the pre-training and fine-tuning procedure precisely. Notably, a DTA model describes a model which is capable of producing predictions for a target and a drug. Therefore, it is unclear what the authors mean with "neural DTA models". It seems like, in the paper, "neural DTA models" describe functional blocks within knn-DTA. ### Novelty - The used Machine Learning techniques (Transformer, KNN, external memory) are not novel. Nevertheless, memory-based methods for DTA applications are promising and worth following. ### Reproducibility Code is not available, therefore this work is hard to reproduce. replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5730 by Reviewer gADj

content.title: Response to Reviewer gADj (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your careful review and valuable comments. We provide the following discussions to respond to your comments. 

> **[-, W1] Error bars and statistical tests are not included. Therefore, performance-wise differences could just arrise by chance which is why the presented results are not relevant. The authors should follow best practices and include error bars and statistical tests.**

**A**:  Thanks for this comment. In preliminary, since our $k$NN retrieval method outputs deterministic results upon a pre-trained DTA model without variance, we don’t report the mean/standard deviation of the $k$NN. As you suggested, we agree that since the pre-trained model contains variance from different seeds training, we still need to report the mean/standard deviation of the results so to evaluate the robustness of $k$NN upon different pre-trained DTA models. Hence, we conducted experiments for $3$ different random seeds. For example, the RMSE mean and standard deviation are $0.684$ and $0.0022$ on BindingDB IC50. These show that $k$NN-DTA achieves good results not by chance and the effectiveness is robust. We have updated the results in Table 1 and 2 accordingly. 

> **[-, W2] Similarity based PCM methods have shown to yield strong performances. Unfortunately, some methods are missing in the evaluation which is why it is unclear whether the proposed architecture reaches state-of-the-art. The authors should include relevant methods such as [1-4]**

**A**: Thanks for the related work. In fact, we have cited most of these works in our initial submission (in section 2), except the Affinity2Vec [1]. Note that these related works only conduct experiments on DAVIS and KIBA datasets, but not on BindingDB. 
* We know these works, but the comparison is not put in Table 2 for some reason. One reason is that the data processing and usage are different from ours. We follow the data processing of DeepPurpose [2], which has split the train/valid/test (7:1:2) sets and provided the processed data. Hence, we take the processed data (https://github.com/kexinhuang12345/DeepPurpose) for our experiments. While other works you provided follow the 5-fold CV setting. Nevertheless, it is weird that [3]’s performance and the result range are largely different (also the reported baselines in their paper) from existing works (DeepDTA [4], DeepCDA [5]), which cannot be compared. Besides, the NerLTR-DTA [4] splits the data into four different settings by seen or unseen of the drugs/targets, while other works (including ours) do not have this constraint. Hence, their work cannot be directly compared either. Also, when we check their codes, some problems arise like no releasing or java code. 
*  To include your comment, we put Affinity2Vec [1] and DeepCDA [4] in Table 2 and update Table 2 accordingly. We can see that our results are still better than most of the works (except Affinity2Vec on KIBA). We then remove the SOTA claim on KIBA. (c) We would like to kindly emphasize that our work focuses on ***“how can we further exploit the potential of these existing pre-trained DL-based DTA models with no or little effort?”***  We are not aiming to design new models (such as these related works), which require building drug/target similarity matrices, extracting features from these matrices, and training the DTA model based on these features. It is known that building a protein similarity matrix is costly and needs an alignment process. We aim to avoid these ways and improve the existing model performance using simple $k$NN embedding retrieval without retraining cost, which is plug-and-play.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer gADj (Part 1)

content.title: Response to Reviewer gADj (Part 2)
content.comment:
> **[-, W3] The authors missed to refer to recent Machine Learning literature which deals with external memory based methods such as [5-7]. The authors should add relevant literature and explain why they decided to use KNNs. More sophisticated ML methods for external memories might even boost the overall performance. This seems underexplored.**

**A**  Thanks for providing more related ML papers. We are familiar with these memory-based networks [5,6,7]. However, the differences between the series works of memory networks and ours are obvious. 
* Memory networks aim to extend the memory during training for previous LSTM-based networks since the memory cell in LSTM is small, which may not be enough. Then the external memory is built for enhancing the LSTM model updating at each time step. 
* The memory module in the memory networks is being written and read frequently. The memories are then trained along with the whole model training, which means the memories are part of the network and must be updated with the supervised training. 
* Indeed, the spirit of memory networks or the way memory networks perform has a close relation to the (self) attention computation module. After Transformer was developed, most of the works turned to Transformer since it is much stronger than LSTM in most cases. Similarly, “Hopfield networks” [8] and Transformer are highly similar, and they are equal to some extent. All of these are not what we focused on. 
* These related works are not included in our submitted version mainly due to the difference are clear, and we guess this is also why the first trial of *k*NN retrieval for embedding-based LM models (*k*NN-LM [9]) does not mention these works. But as you suggested, we have added more discussions about these works in the updated version (Section 2). 
* Again, what we want to do is to ***“exploit the power of pre-trained DTA model and improve the performance with no or the least cost.”*** Our $k$NN-DTA requires no training and is plug-and-play, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of Transformer trained models, which differs from memory networks a lot. Why we chose *k*NN retrieval is that this is a very simple and effective method to improve the model performance. We agree that more sophisticated ML techs can boost performance, but this is exactly the opposite of what we want to achieve: **we want to use an easy way instead of a complex way to boost the model’s performance**. 

> **The clarity is diminished since the authors missed to explain the prediction module in the main paper. The authors should include information here (or point the reviewer to referring passages in case the reviewer missed relevant parts).**

**A**:  For the prediction module, we have introduced the “regression prediction head” in Appendix A.3 (sorry to make you feel unclear since this is in the appendix). Since our pre-trained DTA model is an end-to-end model, the prediction module is the top part of the DTA model, which is a simple $MLP$ layer (two linear transformations and a middle $tanh$ activation) that transforms the concatenated drug feature and target feature to output a regression scalar. To make it clearer, we revised the descriptions and put a figure to show the architecture of DTA model in Appendix A.3. 

> **Pre-Training / Fine-tuning unclarity: In 4.1, the precise training procedure remains unclear. The authors should describe the pre-training and fine-tuning procedure precisely. Notably, a DTA model describes a model which is capable of producing predictions for a target and a drug. Therefore, it is unclear what the authors mean with "neural DTA models". It seems like, in the paper, "neural DTA models" describe functional blocks within knn-DTA.**

**A**: Let's respond as follows.
*  For the pre-training and finetuning in section 4.1, we put the descriptions in Appendix A.3 due to space limitations. A summary is here. The “Pre-trained” model contains one pre-trained molecule encoder and protein encoder, which are both $12$ Transformer layers (trained on Pubchem and Pfam). Since we find that directly concatenating the two encoders together for finetuning DTA is not effective (about $0.854$ RMSE on BindingDB Ki), we add additional $4$ layers above each encoder for finetuning on DTA and then fix the pre-trained $12$ encoder layers (the result is $0.784$ RMSE as shown in Table 1). Since this result is good and competitive, we take this DTA model as our “Pre-trained DTA” (in Table 1) and apply our $k$NN method to this model to evaluate its effectiveness. 
* As for the “neural DTA model”, we just want to emphasize that our $k$NN retrieval is applied upon existing deep neural network-trained DTA models since we build the drug similarity from the embedding space. We revised and removed “neural” according to your suggestion. Thanks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a retrieval method called kNN-DTA, for drug-target binding affinity prediction, which is non-parametric and based on embeddings from pretraining model. This method adopts a label aggregation on the nearest neighbors of drug-target and a representation aggregation on the nearest drug or target, and then combines them to make the final prediction. The evaluations on four benchmark datasets show that this method achieves promising performance in some metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1) English expression is clear and fluent.
2) Experimental results show notable improvement of prediction.

Weakness: 
1) Descriptions of the model should be complete. The authors focus on the retrieval methods, but more details are needed on the pre-training methods. According to Table 1 and 2, the pretrained model without kNN component outperformed other baselines. Is the improvement of prediction mainly due to the pretrained model rather than the proposed kNN component? How about the performance of other baseline models enriched with your kNN component?

2) Some of the results in Table 1 should be aligned with the MONN article. Can the authors explain why they do not report the results of MONN (Ensemble of 30 Models)? This result is clearly better than the best method proposed by the authors. In addition, the authors should provide the results sources or more implementation details for the results in Table 1 and Table 2 baselines. In addition, Table 1 and Table 2 should include the mean and standard deviation across at least 3 experimental runs.

3) Comparison with chemical retrieval (Table 5) might be unfair, since you used datastores to save the embeddings of drugs and targets, but the fingerprints of drugs might be computed in real time. Did you compute the fingerprints of drugs and save them in advance? More details of chemical retrieval should be provided.

4) Some notations are ambiguous (e.g., does the λ in 3.1.1 equal to that in 3.1.3?)

5) The superiority of Ada-KNN-DTA over KNN-DTA is questionable for most datasets.

Thanks a lot for your review effort and the detailed comments and questions. We provide the following discussions with you to help better understand the details. 

> **Descriptions of the model should be complete. The authors focus on the retrieval methods, but more details are needed on the pre-training methods. According to Table 1 and 2, the pretrained model without kNN component outperformed other baselines. Is the improvement of prediction mainly due to the pretrained model rather than the proposed kNN component? How about the performance of other baseline models enriched with your kNN component?**

**A**: Thanks for the concrete questions. Let us respond one-by-one point.
*  We are sorry to make you feel unclear about the pre-training details. Due to the space limitation, we put the pre-training details in Appendix A.3 (as mentioned in Section 4.1). Please kindly check it. We briefly summarize here. The model contains one pre-trained molecule encoder and protein encoder, which are both $12$ Transformer layers (trained on Pubchem and Pfam with masked language modeling objective). Since we find that directly concatenating these two pre-trained encoders together for finetuning DTA is not effective (about $0.854$ RMSE on BindingDB Ki), we add additional $4$ layers above each encoder for finetuning on DTA and then fix the pre-trained $12$ encoder layers (the result is then $0.784$ RMSE as shown in Table 1). Since this result is good and competitive, we take this DTA model as our “Pre-trained DTA” (in Table 1) and apply our $k$NN method to this model to evaluate its effectiveness. 
* As described above, directly using the pre-trained $12$ Transformer encoders for finetuning actually provides not enough benefits for DTA ($0.854$ RMSE is not a competitive result). Our “Pre-trained DTA” with $4$ additional layers finetuned on DTA is good ($0.784$ RMSE). With $k$NN retrieval, the results are further improved ($0.748$ RMSE). Therefore, when we are talking about “improvements”, if we compare with other baseline works, our “Pre-trained DTA” indeed provides improvements, but when further compared with $k$NN, it is also clear that $k$NN retrieval provides non-trivial improvement. So, the improvement is not mainly due to the “Pre-trained DTA” model. 
* We show the $k$NN retrieval is effective in general/other deep learning-trained DTA models. We have applied our $k$NN to the existing best GNN-based model (BACPI [1]) and shown the result in Appendix B.7 (due to space limitation) in our initial submission, RMSE is reduced from $0.815$ to $0.797$ and R is improved from $0.856$ to $0.863$. Further, we also directly apply kNN retrieval on the $12$-layer pre-trained encoders (finetune on DTA and the RMSE is $0.854$ as shown above). With kNN retrieval, the performance is improved to $0.824$ RMSE, which also means our $k$NN component can enhance other DTA baseline models. Moreover, we also add $4$-layer Transformer encoders that are trained from scratch for DTA prediction. These results are summarized as follows. We also add these results in Appendix B.7. 

|Pre-trained DTA| RMSE $\downarrow$ | R $\uparrow$ | 
|---|---|---| 
| 12-layer pre-trained DTA |0.854|0.844| 
|+kNN-DTA | 0.824 | 0.853 |
| 4-layer DTA train from scratch |0.892 | 0.827 | 
|+kNN-DTA |0.872 | 0.836 | 
| BACPI |0.815 | 0.856 | 
|+kNN-DTA |0.797 | 0.863 | 


> **Some of the results in Table 1 should be aligned with the MONN article. Can the authors explain why they do not report the results of MONN (Ensemble of 30 Models)? This result is clearly better than the best method proposed by the authors. In addition, the authors should provide the results sources or more implementation details for the results in Table 1 and Table 2 baselines. In addition, Table 1 and Table 2 should include the mean and standard deviation across at least 3 experimental runs.**

**A**:  Thanks for the questions. We provide the following answers. 
* Yes, we noticed that MONN reported the ensemble results with $30$ models. But MONN only reported ensemble on IC50 (no Ki), and most of the papers do not report the ensemble results. Another point is that $30$ ensemble models are indeed costly and the ensemble setting in MONN is not a common practice, that is, each model in MONN has a different hyper-parameter setting (which is called “parameter+NN” ensemble, averaging predictions over the last $10$ epochs of three networks with different hyper-parameters (i.e., the sizes of the last fully connected layers are different)), then these models make the ensemble. Notably, the ensemble is a general trick that can be applied to all DTA models. Therefore, for a fair comparison, we only report the single model’s performance. According to your suggestion, we then also apply the ensemble to $3$ models with our kNN retrieval (three different random seeds on BindingDB IC50), and the performance is $0.668$ RMSE and $0.894$ R, and we can also see improvements.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer qna3 (Part 1)

content.title: Response to Reviewer qna3 (Part 2)
content.comment:
* As the source of the results, in Table 1, the “Random Forest” and “Deep Affinity” are reported from Deep Affinity paper [2], “DeepDTA” and “MONN” are reported from MONN paper [3], “BACPI” is from its original paper [1]. In Table 2, since the training data is from DeepPurpose [4], the number of these baseline works (e.g., “KronRLS”, “GraphDTA”, “DeepDTA”) is reported by “DeepPurpose” and we directly bring them to our paper. We have revised Table illustrations accordingly.

* Thanks for the good suggestion. Indeed, our kNN retrieval ($k$NN-DTA) can be viewed as a simple post-processing that needs no training, hence for a pre-trained DTA model, the enhanced $k$NN-DTA model outputs a deterministic result without any variance. We also notice some baselines (e.g., DeepAffinity[2], MONN [3]) have no mean and variance reported. That’s why we don’t report mean/standard deviation at first. But we agree that we should still report the mean and standard deviation of the results since the pre-trained models contain variance and we can see the improvements of kNN on these different pre-trained models. Hence, we take $3$ pre-trained DTA models (with different random seeds) and then apply $k$NN-DTA. For example, the results are $0.684 (0.0022)$ RMSE on BindingDB IC50. We have updated the results in the tables. 

> **Comparison with chemical retrieval (Table 5) might be unfair, since you used datastores to save the embeddings of drugs and targets, but the fingerprints of drugs might be computed in real time. Did you compute the fingerprints of drugs and save them in advance? More details of chemical retrieval should be provided.**

**A**: Thanks for the careful comment. Yes, we agree that this comparison may not be so fair. The fingerprint and the similarity of chemical rules are calculated online without being saved in advance. According to your suggestion, we save the calculated fingerprints in advance and calculate the time cost, which takes about $655.73$ mins. We can see that compared with the previous cost ($679.88$ mins), the time saving is not much. We analyzed and thought this is largely due to two reasons, one is that the similarity calculation of RDKit, which can only be conducted on CPU, is not fast. While our embedding retrieval is based on Faiss[5], which can be quickly done on GPU in batch mode. Besides, as for the protein similarity calculation, the alignment process costs hugely, which dominates the cost a lot. We have revised section 5.2 accordingly and more can be found in Appendix B.1. 

> **Some notations are ambiguous (e.g., does the λ in 3.1.1 equal to that in 3.1.3?)**

**A**:  Sorry to let you feel ambiguous. You are right, $\lambda$ in 3.1.1 and 3.1.3 is the same. Actually, we will not use \lambda in label aggregation (3.1.1). The label aggregation is performed only in the final unified framework (3.1.3). We have revised section 3.1.1 accordingly to make it clearer. 

> **The superiority of Ada-KNN-DTA over KNN-DTA is questionable for most datasets.**

**A**: We show that Ada-kNN-DTA further improves $k$NN-DTA on BindingDB IC50 and Ki, but no more improvement on DAVIS and KIBA. As mentioned in Section 4.4, we try to give some hypotheses that the centralized data distributions may hinder learning ability. However, the main contribution of our work is from the $k$NN retrieval ($k$NN-DTA), and the Ada-$k$NN-DTA is only an extension. At least, it performs as well as $k$NN-DTA. From a practical view, we can choose Ada-$k$NN-DTA for a slight training, but $k$NN-DTA without training is also strong enough to make improvements. Therefore, we hope this can be kindly acknowledged.
___
**Finally**, as for the novelty. We would like to have some discussions here. First, we use kNN-retrieval from two different spaces, which are the label and representation spaces, and we integrate them into a unified framework. Besides, the extension Ada-$k$NN-DTA provides a slight training version, which can further improve to some extent (but not on all datasets). We also want to kindly emphasize that we are the first work to apply embedding-based $K$NN-retrieval in DTA prediction. Since affinity prediction is highly crucial, we deliver the message to chemists that using simple embedding retrieval (post-processing) upon DL models can do well in DTA prediction. We hope to benefit/inspire more people (especially for AI4Science researchers) to do more advanced innovations.

Thanks again and we hope the above answers can help remove your concerns and questions.

content.title: Paper revision summary
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and AC,

Thanks for your effort in reviewing our submission. According to your comments and suggestions, we have made revisions to our submission. Below is a quick overview of what we have changed in the manuscript (all detailed changes in our manuscript have been colored blue).

* We added more **details of the datasets** (especially the label $y$) in Appendix A.1.
* We added more descriptions **about the pre-trained DTA models** which contain the pre-trained encoders using Transformer, the detailed model architecture (shown in Figure 4), and also the pre-training method in Appendix A.3.
* We added more details of the **compared baseline methods**. We discussed more related works (Section 2) that reviewers pointed out and compared with them in the tables (Section 4). We added the sources of the reported baseline models in the tables. 
* We added the **mean and standard deviation** of the model performances and listed them in the main tables (Table 1 and 2). 
* We added more experiments for applying **$k$NN-DTA on different pre-trained DTA models** to show universal effectiveness. The results are in Appendix B.7.
* We updated the **chemical similarity retrieval** experiments to make them fairer (Section 5.2 and Appendix B.1). 
* We have revised some typos and formulations that reviewers suggested. We also make some descriptions clearer for scientific understanding. 

Thanks for checking the updated version.

Best,
Authors.
